title: What must employers verify and record for Working with Children Checks in NSW, Victoria and Queensland?
description: What NSW, Victorian and Queensland employers must verify and record for Working with Children Checks and blue cards, with penalties, as at November 2026.
shortAnswer: A Working with Children Check is a screening clearance, not a training requirement. In New South Wales the employer must register with the Office of the Children's Guardian, verify each worker online and keep a record of each verification. In Victoria the organization must check status before work starts under the Worker Screening Act 2020. In Queensland the organization must link each worker to its blue card account and keep an employee register.
keyTakeaways: Screening and training are separate obligations: a valid check shows a person has been cleared, not that they have been trained in child safety, reporting or the organization's code of conduct.

NSW employers must register, verify both the application number and the clearance number (the education sector must verify the clearance number), re-verify after the five year renewal, and record seven details per worker.
Victorian organizations may only engage a person who holds a WWC Clearance, has a pending application or is exempt, and paid staff must hold an Employee clearance rather than a Volunteer one.
Queensland's rule is "No Card. No Link. No Start.": failing to have a worker hold a blue card and be linked before starting carries a maximum of 200 penalty units ($34,540) or 2 years in prison.

Evidence an auditor will ask for is the verification or link record, the expiry date and the action taken on any status change, so the screening register should sit alongside, not inside, the training matrix.
jurisdiction: Australia (New South Wales, Victoria and Queensland)
regulator: Office of the Children's Guardian (NSW); Social Services Regulator, through Working with Children Check Victoria (Victoria); Blue Card Services (Queensland)
appliesTo: Schools, early childhood education and care services, outside school hours care and tutoring providers
Sporting, cultural and religious organizations, camps and other bodies providing services to children
Employers and volunteer organizations engaging adults in child-related work, including contractors and students on placement where state rules require it
Self-employed people and sole traders in child-related work

sections.heading: Is a Working with Children Check a training requirement?

blocks.text: No. A Working with Children Check (WWCC) is a pre-engagement and ongoing screening clearance issued by a state or territory regulator, and it says nothing about what a person knows. Each Australian state runs its own scheme under its own Act, so the employer duties differ by state even though the purpose is the same.

The distinction matters for compliance teams because the evidence is different. A training record shows a person completed and passed specific content. A screening record shows the employer confirmed, with the regulator, that the person was cleared to work with children on a given date. Neither substitutes for the other: a cleared worker still needs training in reporting obligations (see [mandatory reporting training in Australia](/regulations/mandatory-reporting-training-australia)) and in the child safe standards that apply to the organization (see [Victoria's Child Safe Standards](/regulations/victoria-child-safe-standards-training)).

The NSW Office of the Children's Guardian makes the same point from the other direction. Its [employer guidance](https://www.ocg.nsw.gov.au/working-children-check/organisation/role-employer) says organizations "must not rely on the Check in lieu of other child safe strategies" by asking workers who are not engaged in child-related work to have a Check.

blocks.title: Currency
blocks.text: This page reflects regulator guidance as at November 2026 for New South Wales, Victoria and Queensland only. Other states and territories run separate schemes with different rules. Penalty amounts change with penalty unit values each financial year.

sections.heading: What must NSW employers do under the Working with Children Check?

blocks.text: NSW employers must register as a child-related employer, identify which roles need a Check, verify clearances and renewals online, and keep records. The Office of the Children's Guardian (OCG) states that "it is against the law to engage anyone in child-related work without a Working with Children Check" and that verifying "is a legal requirement and there is a fine for not verifying".

items: **Register:** complete the online employer form and nominate 2 officials authorized to receive confidential information, who are notified if a worker becomes barred. Sole traders with no employees do not register; they give their details to clients to verify.

**Verify:** check new workers first by Application (APP) number and then by clearance number. The OCG notes an exception: in the education sector a clearance number is required, so an APP number alone is not enough.
**Re-verify:** verify again when a worker renews after 5 years. Workers can renew up to 3 months before expiry, and employers are expected to remind them.
**No self-verification:** the person who verifies others must have their own Check verified by someone else in the organization.
**Act on status:** a person may only be engaged if the status is "Cleared" or "Application in progress". Anyone barred, interim barred, not found or expired must be removed from child-related work.

blocks.text: According to the OCG's [register and verify guidance](https://www.ocg.nsw.gov.au/working-children-check/wwcc-information-organisations/help-register-and-verify), verification "must be done through our online WWCC system and you must keep a record of each verification". The Employer Portal generates a verification history file on the first day of each month covering the previous month, which is a convenient audit extract.

The OCG runs a [compliance program](https://www.ocg.nsw.gov.au/working-children-check/wwcc-information-organisations/working-children-check-compliance-program) that requests and analyzes employer WWCC records, conducts audit visits and investigates non-compliance, with penalty infringement notices available. The OCG notes its compliance and enforcement policy is under review in 2026.

sections.heading: What must Victorian organizations check under the Worker Screening Act 2020?

blocks.text: Victorian organizations must check a worker's status before work starts and may only engage a person who holds a WWC Clearance, has lodged an application that is being assessed, or has a relevant exemption. The [Worker Screening Act 2020](https://www.vic.gov.au/legislation-wwc-check) commenced on February 1, 2021, replacing the Working with Children Act 2005.
The Victorian Government's [legal obligations page](https://www.vic.gov.au/legal-obligations-organisations) lists what an organization must do. The points with the most compliance weight are:

items: Do not allow anyone to do child-related work without a clearance, or while subject to an interim WWC Exclusion, Exclusion, Interim Bar or Suspension.
Ensure paid workers hold an Employee WWC Clearance, not a Volunteer WWC Clearance.
Know when each worker's and volunteer's clearance expires, and use the Working with Children Status Checker to confirm status.
Do not offer an unscreened person's services to another organization for child-related work.

blocks.text: Seeing a card is not enough. The [staff clearances guidance](https://www.vic.gov.au/you-staffs-WWC-clearances) says the organization must check the worker has added the organization's name to their details through Service Victoria, and should record the number, expiry date and card type ('E' for paid employees or 'V' for volunteers). Workers must notify the regulator within 21 days of starting child-related work with an organization. A worker given a WWC Exclusion must tell the organization in writing within seven days.

Teachers currently registered with the Victorian Institute of Teaching are exempt from holding a Check unless they have been given a WWC Exclusion, according to the [teacher information page](https://www.vic.gov.au/victorian-teacher-information). Other listed exemptions include people under 18, parents volunteering in an activity their child participates in, and students aged 18 or 19 volunteering through their own educational institution.

blocks.title: In transition
blocks.text: The Victorian Government states that reforms taking effect in July 2026 allow child safety risk information to be obtained and considered in WWC assessments and re-assessments. The Social Services Regulator can now issue an Interim Bar or Suspension for up to two years while it assesses that information, and notifies organizations the worker has told it about.

sections.heading: What must Queensland organizations do under the blue card system?

blocks.text: Queensland organizations must ensure each worker holds a current blue card (or has applied for an exemption card) and is linked to the organization before regulated work starts, and must keep an employee register. Queensland describes the system as regulated under the Working with Children Check Act 2000 and the Working with Children (Risk Management and Screening) Regulation 2020, and states that card holders are monitored every day using Queensland Police Service information ([blue card system explained](https://www.qld.gov.au/jobs/blue-card/system/system-explained)).

Queensland's [organization obligations page](https://www.qld.gov.au/jobs/blue-card/organisations/blue-card-obligations-for-organisations) states that you "must link an applicant or blue card or exemption card holder before they start child-related work" and that links must be removed when a person leaves. New volunteer and student applicants must be linked before they submit their application, which confirms their status and gives them access to a free card.

Where a person does not need a card, the register must record why they are exempt ([penalties for organizations](https://www.qld.gov.au/jobs/blue-card/system/offences-and-penalties/organisations)).

sections.heading: How do screening obligations map to roles, timing and audit evidence?

blocks.text: The practical answer is a single screening register with one row per worker per state, kept beside the training matrix and reconciled against payroll and volunteer rosters. blocks.text: Two design points reduce audit findings. First, record the verification date and outcome, not just the card number, because the obligation is to verify with the regulator. Second, drive renewal reminders from the expiry date field, as the [refresh cycle guide](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles) describes for training, so that no one works past expiry. The [audit preparation guide](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit) covers how to package the register with training records.

sections.heading: Which training should sit alongside a Working with Children Check?

blocks.text: A WWCC tells an employer who may be engaged; the training program has to cover how cleared people behave once engaged. For schools and early childhood services, that usually means training on the organization's child safe code of conduct, recognizing and reporting harm, and the role specific reporting duties set by state law.

items: **Screening process training** for the people who run it: how to verify, how to read each status, what to do on a bar or suspension notice, and how to protect worker privacy.
**Child safety and reporting training** for all workers in child-related roles, mapped to the applicable child safe standards and reporting law.
**Manager training** on acting promptly when a regulator notifies a status change, since the employer, not a third-party verifier, is responsible for removing the person.

blocks.text: Placing screening and training in the same [training matrix](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix) as separate columns makes gaps visible: a worker who is cleared but untrained, or trained but with an expired check, shows up immediately.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry treats screening clearances and training as distinct obligations in the framework, each with its own evidence type and owner. Child safety training is then built from the obligations that apply in each state, so the record shows both that a person was cleared and what they were assessed on.

faqs.q: Can a worker start before their NSW clearance is issued?
faqs.a: Generally yes, once the employer has verified their Application (APP) number and the status shows "Application in progress". The OCG notes that the education sector is an exception: a clearance number is required there, so schools should not rely on an APP number alone. The employer must verify again when the clearance number is issued.

faqs.q: Does a Victorian volunteer clearance cover paid work?
faqs.a: No. Victorian organizations must ensure paid workers doing child-related work hold an Employee WWC Clearance rather than a Volunteer WWC Clearance. Service Victoria offers an upgrade from volunteer to employee status, and the organization should record the card type ('E' or 'V') to show it checked.

faqs.q: Can an employer outsource WWCC verification in NSW?
faqs.a: An employer can engage a third party, but the OCG does not endorse or authorize third-party verifiers and they get no extra system access. The employer must still register, and if a worker is barred the OCG notifies the employer, which remains responsible for removing the person from child-related work.

faqs.q: Is a check from one state valid in another?
faqs.a: Each state's clearance is issued under that state's law, and the employer duties on this page are framed around that state's own clearance or card. An organization operating across NSW, Victoria and Queensland should confirm with each regulator which clearance a worker needs for work performed in that state, and keep separate register entries.
